title: Concurrency Pattern: Fan-In / Fan-Out
summary: **Fan-out** starts several goroutines reading from one source channel to parallelize work; **fan-in** merges several channels back into one so a single consumer can read all results. Together they're how Go scales a stage horizontally — the tricky part is closing the merged channel exactly once, which a WaitGroup handles.

subtopics.title: Fan-out: many readers, one channel
subtopics.explanation: Launch N goroutines that all receive from the same input channel. Each value is delivered to exactly one of them, so the work is spread across goroutines automatically. This is how you parallelize a slow stage.
subtopics.example: for i := 0; i < N; i++ { go process(in, out) }

subtopics.title: Fan-in: merge many channels into one
subtopics.explanation: When several goroutines each produce on their own output channel, fan-in copies all of those into a single channel so one consumer can range over everything. A merge function with a WaitGroup is the canonical implementation.

subtopics.title: The single-closer principle
subtopics.explanation: A channel must be closed by exactly one goroutine and never written to after close. In fan-in, each forwarding goroutine must NOT close the merged channel; instead a WaitGroup waits for all of them, then one goroutine closes it once.

subtopics.title: Merging with a WaitGroup
subtopics.explanation: merge() adds one to a WaitGroup per input channel, launches a goroutine per channel that forwards values into the merged channel and calls wg.Done() when its input closes, and a final goroutine closes merged after wg.Wait().
subtopics.example: wg.Add(len(cs)); for _, c := range cs { go forward(c) }

subtopics.title: select-based merge
subtopics.explanation: For a small fixed number of channels you can merge with a single select loop instead of N goroutines, but you must track which inputs have closed (set them to nil to disable that case) to avoid busy-looping.
subtopics.example: case v, ok := <-a: if !ok { a = nil; continue }

subtopics.title: Ordering is not preserved
subtopics.explanation: Fan-out/fan-in maximizes throughput but scrambles order: values come back as workers finish, not as they entered. If you need order, tag items with an index and reassemble, or don't fan out that stage.
subtopics.example: type item struct{ idx int; val T }

foundations.overview: Fan-out and fan-in are two halves of the same idea: spread work across goroutines to go faster, then collect the results back into a single stream. Fan-out is just multiple goroutines all receiving from one input channel — the runtime hands each value to one free worker, so a slow stage now runs in parallel. Fan-in is the reverse: several producer channels are merged into one so a single consumer can read them all. The merge step is where most bugs hide, because the merged channel must be closed exactly once, only after every producer has finished — which is what a WaitGroup is for.
foundations.formalDefinition: Fan-out is the distribution of one channel's values across multiple consumer goroutines for parallelism; fan-in is the multiplexing of multiple producer channels into a single channel, with a WaitGroup ensuring the merged channel is closed exactly once after all producers complete.
foundations.whyItMatters: It's the canonical way to parallelize a pipeline stage in Go and to recombine results, and it directly tests the things interviewers probe: channel ownership, the single-closer rule, and leak-free shutdown.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a highway toll plaza: one lane of cars (input) fans out into several toll booths (workers) so they're served in parallel, then the lanes merge back into one road (fan-in). Cars exit in whatever order their booth finished — order is not preserved.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Fan-out relies on the runtime delivering each channel send to exactly one waiting receiver. Fan-in spawns one forwarding goroutine per source; each blocks on its source until closed, then returns; a final goroutine blocks on wg.Wait() and closes the merged channel, after which the consumer's range ends.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Parallelizing CPU-heavy transforms in a stream, querying multiple backends at once and merging their responses, aggregating logs/metrics from many producers into one sink.
foundations.businessImpact: Parallelizing the slowest stage cuts end-to-end latency and raises throughput on existing hardware, deferring the need to scale out and lowering cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A clean merge() helper makes fan-in reusable and the single-closer discipline keeps shutdown deterministic; getting ownership right prevents the panics and leaks that plague ad-hoc concurrency.
foundations.performanceImpact: Fan-out speedup is bounded by the slowest stage and by how parallelizable the work is (Amdahl's law); too many workers add scheduling and channel contention without further gains.
commonUseCases: Parallelizing a single slow pipeline stage with N workers (fan-out)
Merging results from multiple workers into one consumer (fan-in)
Scatter/gather: query several services concurrently and combine
Aggregating many event sources into a single processed stream

commonMisconceptions.myth: Each forwarding goroutine should close the merged channel when its input ends.
commonMisconceptions.reality: That closes the channel multiple times (panic) and while others still send (panic). Only one goroutine closes it, after wg.Wait().

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fan-out preserves the order of the input.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Values are processed and emitted as workers finish, so order is lost. Tag items with an index if you must reassemble order.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More fan-out workers always means faster.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Speedup is capped by the parallelizable fraction of work and downstream capacity; beyond that, extra goroutines only add overhead.

steps.name: Count the inputs
steps.detail: wg.Add(len(channels)) — one outstanding forwarder per source channel.

steps.name: Launch forwarders
steps.detail: For each source, a goroutine ranges over it, copying every value into the merged channel.

steps.name: Forwarder finishes
steps.detail: When a source closes, its range ends, the forwarder calls wg.Done() and returns.

steps.name: Wait then close
steps.detail: A separate goroutine blocks on wg.Wait(); once all forwarders are done it close(merged) — exactly once.

steps.name: Consumer drains
steps.detail: The single consumer ranges over merged and exits when the close arrives. No goroutine is left blocked.

interactiveExamples.title: fan-out + fan-in end to end
interactiveExamples.explanation: gen produces numbers; we fan out to 3 square workers each reading the same input; merge fans their outputs back into one channel that main sums. Note merge uses a WaitGroup and closes the merged channel exactly once.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: the merge panics — make it close once
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each forwarder wrongly closes the merged channel, causing 'close of closed channel' and 'send on closed channel' panics. Replace the per-forwarder close with a single WaitGroup-driven close.

checkpoints.prompt: In fan-out, what happens when N goroutines all receive from the same channel?
options: Every goroutine gets a copy of each value
Each value goes to exactly one of the goroutines
Only the first goroutine receives anything
It panics — a channel can't have multiple receivers
checkpoints.explanation: A channel delivers each sent value to exactly one receiver. With multiple goroutines receiving, the runtime hands each value to one free receiver, spreading the work — that's fan-out.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this merge panic with 'send on closed channel'?
options: Both forwarders close out; the second close (and any send racing it) panics
checkpoints.explanation: Two goroutines each close out. The second close panics ('close of closed channel'), and a forwarder still sending while the other closes panics with 'send on closed channel'. Close must happen once, via wg.Wait().

checkpoints.prompt: After fanning out a sequence 1,2,3,4 to several workers and fanning the results back in, the consumer prints them. What can you rely on?
options: The same multiset of values, but in nondeterministic order
checkpoints.explanation: Fan-out/fan-in preserves the set of values but not their order — items emerge as workers finish. If order matters, tag each item with an index and reassemble.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the merge so the output channel is closed exactly once after all forwarders finish.
checkpoints.explanation: A dedicated goroutine blocks on wg.Wait() until every forwarder has finished sending, then closes out exactly once. Closing before Wait would panic on in-flight sends; closing inline blocks the merge.

codeLab.title: Implement a generic channel merge (fan-in)
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Merge(cs ...<-chan int) <-chan int` that fans in any number of input channels into one output channel, closing the output exactly once after all inputs are drained. The harness sends on several channels and checks the merged multiset.
hints: wg.Add(len(cs)) once, then launch one forwarding goroutine per channel that defers wg.Done().
Each forwarder ranges over its input and forwards into the shared out channel.
Close out in a separate goroutine after wg.Wait() — never inside the forwarders, or you double-close.

debuggingLab.title: The merged channel never closes (consumer hangs)
debuggingLab.symptom: The consumer's `for v := range merged` never ends; the program hangs at exit.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The WaitGroup counter is never incremented, so wg.Wait() returns immediately (counter is already 0). close(out) then runs while forwarders are still sending — that either panics with 'send on closed channel', or, if the close beats the sends, the consumer stops early and the forwarders block forever sending into a closed/unread channel. Either way the lifecycle is broken: Add must match the number of Done calls.
commonMistakes: Forgetting wg.Add(len(cs)) (or calling Add inside the goroutine, racing Wait).
Closing the merged channel before all forwarders have finished.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add wg.Add(len(cs)) before launching the forwarders so Wait blocks until all are done.

solution.expectedOutput: (merged channel closes after all inputs drain; consumer's range ends cleanly)

theory.question: Explain fan-out and fan-in and how they combine.
theory.directAnswer: Fan-out means launching multiple goroutines that all receive from one input channel, so the work is processed in parallel — each value goes to exactly one worker. Fan-in is the reverse: a merge function combines several output channels into one, so a single consumer can read all results. Combined, you parallelize a stage (fan-out) and then recollect its results (fan-in), with a WaitGroup ensuring the merged channel closes exactly once.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two complementary channel patterns: distribute one channel to many goroutines, then multiplex many channels into one.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To scale a slow pipeline stage horizontally while keeping a simple single-consumer interface.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Multiple receivers on one channel split the load; a merge goroutine per source forwards into a shared channel that a watcher closes after wg.Wait().

theory.whyImportant: It's the standard Go scaling pattern and a direct test of channel ownership and shutdown correctness.
theory.realWorldExample: A scatter/gather handler queries three replicas concurrently (fan-out) and merges whichever respond into one result stream (fan-in).

nestedTopics.title: Single-closer principle
nestedTopics.explanation: Exactly one goroutine closes the merged channel; forwarders never close it, or you get double-close/send-on-closed panics.

nestedTopics.title: Order loss
nestedTopics.explanation: Results arrive as workers finish, not in input order; tag with an index to reassemble if needed.

followUps.question: Who owns and closes the merged channel?
followUps.answer: The merge function does, via a single goroutine that closes it once after wg.Wait(); the forwarders only send and signal Done.

followUps.question: Does fan-out guarantee even load distribution?
followUps.answer: No explicit balancing — the runtime delivers each value to whichever receiver is ready, which is approximately fair but not exactly even.

theory.question: How do you preserve input order when fanning out work across goroutines?
theory.directAnswer: Fan-out inherently loses order, so you reintroduce it explicitly: tag each item with its original index before fan-out, then on fan-in write results into a pre-sized slice at that index (no lock needed since indices are distinct), or buffer out-of-order results in a map keyed by index and emit them in sequence. If strict streaming order is required, that stage usually can't be parallelized.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reassembly strategy layered on top of unordered fan-out/fan-in.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Parallelism trades ordering for throughput; some consumers need order back.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Carry the index with each unit of work; place each result at result[idx], or reorder via a small buffer keyed by sequence number.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing the order trade-off and how to recover it is a common senior-level probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Parallel image resizing where the gallery must display thumbnails in upload order — each job carries its index and results land at that slice position.

nestedTopics.title: Indexed slice
nestedTopics.explanation: Pre-size results and write each at its index; distinct indices mean no data race and no mutex.

nestedTopics.title: Reorder buffer
nestedTopics.explanation: For streaming, hold results in a map by sequence and flush in order as the next expected index arrives.

followUps.question: Is writing to distinct slice indices from goroutines safe?
followUps.answer: Yes — different indices are different memory; only the backing array is shared and never resized, so no race.

scenario.question: Your fan-in code intermittently panics in production with 'send on closed channel'. Where do you look?
scenario.directAnswer: A goroutine is sending on the merged channel after it's been closed, which means the channel was closed too early or by the wrong goroutine. Check that only one goroutine closes the merged channel and only after wg.Wait(); verify wg.Add count matches the number of forwarders and that each forwarder defers Done so close can't run while a send is in flight. Also confirm no consumer or unrelated code closes the channel.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A channel-ownership violation surfacing as an intermittent panic.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Closing while sends are outstanding, or closing from multiple goroutines, is a data race on the channel's state.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: close marks the channel closed; any concurrent or subsequent send panics, which is timing-dependent and thus intermittent.

scenario.whyImportant: send/close-on-closed panics are common, hard to reproduce, and crash the process.
scenario.realWorldExample: Each forwarder closed the merged channel on its own; under load two closes raced, panicking the service.

nestedTopics.title: Single closer
nestedTopics.explanation: Centralize the close in one watcher goroutine after wg.Wait(); never close from forwarders or receivers.

nestedTopics.title: defer Done
nestedTopics.explanation: Deferring Done guarantees the forwarder's last send completes before its Done, so Wait won't release the closer prematurely.

followUps.question: How do you reproduce such a timing bug reliably?
followUps.answer: Run the test under `go test -race -count=100` and with GOMAXPROCS>1; the race detector flags concurrent close/send on the channel state.

coding.question: Implement `func FanOutFanIn(in <-chan int, workers int, f func(int) int) <-chan int` that fans `in` out to `workers` goroutines applying f, then fans the results into one output channel (order need not be preserved).
coding.thoughtProcess: Launch `workers` goroutines, each ranging over the shared input channel and sending f(v) on its own contribution to a shared output. Use a WaitGroup to know when all workers have drained `in`, then a single goroutine closes the output. The shared input gives fan-out; sending into one output gives fan-in without a separate merge step.
coding.lineByLine: We start `workers` goroutines that each range over the same input channel — the runtime hands each value to one worker, which is the fan-out. Every worker sends its transformed value into the single `out` channel, which is the fan-in. The WaitGroup counts the workers; once `in` is closed and all workers finish their range loops they each call Done, the watcher's wg.Wait() returns, and it closes `out` exactly once so the consumer's range ends cleanly.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n/workers) wall-clock for n items when work is parallelizable.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(workers) goroutines plus the channel buffers.

alternativeApproaches.title: Separate merge step
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Give each worker its own output channel and combine them with a reusable merge(cs ...<-chan int) helper — more composable when stages are built independently.

alternativeApproaches.title: errgroup for errors
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If f can fail, run workers under errgroup.Group with SetLimit(workers) to bound concurrency and cancel on the first error.

followUps.question: Why is closing `in`'s responsibility on the caller, not this function?
followUps.answer: The function only receives from `in`; the channel's owner (the sender) must close it. Receivers never close a channel they don't own.

followUps.question: How would you preserve order here?
followUps.answer: Change the element type to carry an index, then have the consumer place each result at out[idx] instead of streaming.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Treat each channel as owned by exactly one goroutine that creates and closes it (sender-closes, single-closer). Build a reusable merge() helper rather than re-implementing fan-in per call site. Thread a context through stages so the whole scatter/gather can be cancelled together.
productionDeepDive.performance: Fan-out speedup is capped by the parallelizable fraction (Amdahl) and downstream limits; benchmark to find the worker count where added goroutines stop helping. Unbuffered channels add a synchronization point per item — a small buffer can cut handoff overhead on hot paths.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: The single-closer principle is the crux: forwarders only send and Done; one watcher closes after wg.Wait(). Run with -race; a 'send on closed channel' panic almost always means a close happened too early or from the wrong goroutine.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Give every forwarder/worker a guaranteed exit (its source gets closed) plus a select on ctx.Done() for early cancellation, so a stalled upstream can't strand goroutines. Recover panics in worker bodies so one bad item doesn't crash the pipeline.
productionDeepDive.observability: Expose per-stage throughput and goroutine counts; alert on monotonic NumGoroutine growth (a forwarder whose source never closes leaks). pprof goroutine profiles pinpoint stuck forwarders by line.
productionDeepDive.security: Bound fan-out so adversarial input volume can't translate into unbounded goroutines (a DoS vector); apply per-item timeouts via context so one slow/malicious item can't tie up a worker indefinitely.

caseStudies.problem: Query many shards and combine results with low latency.
caseStudies.solution: Fan out one request per shard, fan in responses, return when enough arrive.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Tail latency vs. completeness — sometimes you return after k of n respond.
caseStudies.lessons: Pair fan-in with deadlines so a slow shard can't hold the whole response.

caseStudies.problem: Aggregate many producer streams into one processed sink.
caseStudies.solution: A WaitGroup-driven merge that closes the sink once all producers end.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Ordering is lost across producers; acceptable for aggregations.
caseStudies.lessons: Single-closer discipline keeps shutdown clean even with dozens of producers.

keyTakeaways: Fan-out = many goroutines receiving from one channel (parallelism); fan-in = merging many channels into one (single consumer).
The merged channel must be closed exactly once, by one goroutine, only after wg.Wait() — forwarders just send and call Done.
Order is not preserved across fan-out; tag items with an index and reassemble (e.g. write to result[idx]) if you need it back.
Give every goroutine a guaranteed exit, run with -race to catch send/close-on-closed bugs, and bound fan-out to avoid DoS-via-goroutines.
